# Vendoring `rars`

`vendor/rars/` is a curated copy of the `rars` crate from our perf fork of
[bitplane/rars](https://github.com/bitplane/rars). It is **not** a git subtree
or submodule — it is a mirrored subset, produced by
[`sync-from-fork.sh`](sync-from-fork.sh).

Upstream-tracking policy is FREEZE + cherry-pick: watch the fork for decoder
fixes, port selectively, re-run the gates, then re-vendor.

## What is vendored

| Path | Source in fork | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `src/**` | `crates/rars/src/**` | exact mirror (`rsync --delete`) |
| `tests/fixtures/**` | `crates/rars/tests/fixtures/**` | **exact mirror — all of it** |
| `COPYING` | **not synced - ours** | states this fork's MIT OR Apache-2.0 and why; see below |
| `LICENSE-MIT`, `LICENSE-APACHE` | **not synced - ours** | the two texts upstream does not ship |
| `Cargo.toml` | `crates/rars/Cargo.toml` | **hand-maintained, see below** |

Not vendored: `tests/*.rs` (fork integration tests — we run only the inline
`--lib` tests), `benches/`, `fuzz/`, `python/`, `scripts/`, `target/`.

## Why `tests/fixtures/**` must always come along

The rars unit tests live **inline** in `src/lib.rs` and load inputs via
`env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")/tests/fixtures/rar15_40/...`. If any referenced
fixture is missing, `cargo test -p rars --lib` fails with `NotFound` on a clean
checkout.

This exact bug shipped once: an earlier sync copied `src/` but dropped
`tests/fixtures/`, and it was hotfixed by hand-vendoring only the two fixtures
the then-current tests happened to read. Hand-picking fixtures re-introduces the
same fragility — the next inline test that references a third fixture breaks
again. So the sync mirrors the **whole** fixtures tree; do not trim it to a
subset.

## Re-vendoring to a newer fork rev

```sh
# 1. Sync src/ + tests/fixtures/ + COPYING from your fork checkout.
RARS_FORK=~/path/to/rars ./vendor/rars/sync-from-fork.sh

# 2. Reconcile Cargo.toml BY HAND *only if* the fork's [dependencies] changed.
#    The vendored manifest deliberately differs from the fork's:
#      - de-workspaced deps (concrete versions, not `.workspace = true`)
#      - version = "0.4.6+nzbfast"
#      - [lints.rust] unsafe_code = "deny" (was forbid until the NEON
#        blake2sp entry, 22 Aug 2026), unused_must_use = "deny"
#      - no [dev-dependencies], no [[bench]] (not vendored)
#    The script never overwrites Cargo.toml, so it survives a re-sync.

# 3. Gate: must stay green.
cargo test -p rars --lib

# 4. Commit.
git add -A vendor/rars
git commit -m "vendor/rars: sync to fork rev <rev>"
```

## Local divergences (re-apply after every sync)

`sync-from-fork.sh` mirrors `src/**` with `rsync --delete`, so anything we
change under `src/` is GONE the moment someone re-vendors. Keep the ledger
below current, and walk it after every sync. Each entry names a marker
comment carrying the same date, so `git grep 'nzbfast-local change'` under
`vendor/rars/src` finds what should be here.

**A new entry goes in THIS table, newest first - not in "What is
vendored" above, which lists PATHS and how they are mirrored.** Between
`40d85a1a88` (7 Sep 2026) and 8 Sep 2026, 64 divergence rows were
appended to that first table instead, because it is the first one a
reader scrolling to append meets; they are back here now. A row filed
there is not merely untidy - the re-vendor walk this section exists for
reads THIS table, so those 64 changes would have been silently dropped
on the next `sync-from-fork.sh`. The table below must also stay ONE
table: a blank line between rows ends it in Markdown, and one had crept
in five rows from the bottom.

| Date | What | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2026-09-11 | **`Gf16MulTable::new` builds its split byte tables by a SUBSET WALK over the field's xtime chain** rather than by 512 `Gf16::mul` calls. Multiplication by a fixed coefficient is GF(2)-linear in its other operand, so every entry of the 256-entry `lo`/`hi` pair is the XOR of the sixteen `c * x^k` chain elements its index has bits set for: ~16 shifts and 510 XORs over a 1 KiB working set, where the log/antilog form was 512 branchy round trips through the module's 768 KiB `exp`/`log` pair. New `power_chain` / `split_tables` free functions, derived from this module's own `PRIMITIVE_POLYNOMIAL` rather than copied from the PAR2 engine's gf16 (the two fields turn out to be the same, which is a coincidence nobody should have to re-check). `Gf16MulTable::new` loses its now-unused `&Gf16` parameter across all six call sites, and with it three dead `let gf = shared_gf16()` bindings. Measured on the dev Mac, two binaries interleaved with the order flipped every rep: the table build is 616 -> 147 ns, worth **-30.3%** on an end-to-end `repair_shards_striped` at a 20,900-byte stripe and **-19.9%** at 41,700 (within-arm spread 3.5% and 1.4%), and NOTHING on a 1 GiB `-rr3` create, which caches per shard and pays only 1,200 builds for the whole archive. The striped repair is the site that matters because it rebuilds per (source, damaged row) PER STRIPE, and nzbfast's `repair_cap()` floor of 8 MiB divided by heavy damage makes a stripe tens of KiB. | 2026-09-08 | The Huffman tree is built from TWO QUEUES rather than a binary heap (van Leeuwen). Once the leaves are sorted the merged sums come out non-decreasing on their own, so the next-smallest node is always at the head of one of the two queues and the heap's sift work disappears; the heap re-sifted about 400 symbols for every table of every block. **Output is byte-identical and that is checked end to end, not just asserted**: a 24 MiB mixed fixture creates the same archive to the byte with and without this (same sha256, same 3,496,529 bytes). Tie-breaking is the thing that could have moved it, so both queues carry `(frequency, order)` and compare as whole tuples - a leaf's `order` is always below a merged node's, so a frequency tie still resolves to the leaf exactly as popping the heap did - and `the_two_queue_builder_matches_the_heap_on_ties_and_saturated_sums` differentials 512 cases against the reference builder with case classes that force heavy ties and force `saturating_add` to actually saturate. Measured 3.2% off whole-archive creation on a mixed 4 GiB corpus and 10.0% on repetitive text; treat 3.2% as representative, because repetitive text rebuilds tables far more often per byte. The 10.0% arm ran interleaved against a same-binary A/A control that moved 0.93%, so it is an order of magnitude outside the noise. Candidate from the review's unmerged RAR5 shortlist. | `src/codec/huffman.rs` |
| 2026-09-08 | The streamed writer PARKS AND REUSES its encoder workers. A set of small members spawned one scoped thread per member; workers now wait on a channel and are handed the next member's bytes, so a thread launch is paid once per worker rather than once per member. Measured: 4 GiB / 4,096 mixed members 3.5% faster, 1 GiB repetitive 24.8%, a 32-fixture diversity screen 2.8% - and 0.4%, ie nothing, at 64 large members. The win is thread launches, so it scales with member COUNT and not archive size; the headline number hides that. **Carries a fix the original candidate did not have.** A parked worker is never joined, and `std::thread::scope` panics at its end whenever a thread panicked and nothing consumed the panic (`join` consumes it by taking the result out of the packet; a channel recv does not), so a panicking encoder would have panicked PAST the `InvalidHeader` error `drain_one` builds and that error would never have reached a caller. The worker body is wrapped in `catch_unwind` and converts at the site. `the_streamed_writer_reports_a_panicking_encoder_as_an_error` covers it through the real writer using a test-only member marker rather than a process-global flag another concurrent test could consume, and it was verified as a real test: with the `catch_unwind` removed it fails with "the writer PANICKED instead of returning an error". | 2026-09-07 | ADAPTIVE ENTROPY-BLOCK BOUNDARIES on the RAR 5 writer, ON by default (`codec::rar50::boundaries`, new; `EncodeOptions::adaptive_entropy_blocks` and `WriterOptions::adaptive_entropy_blocks`, both `true`, `rar5cli --fixed-entropy-blocks` for the other arm). A tokenizer block's token stream was cut into entropy blocks every `ENTROPY_BLOCK_BYTES` (256 KiB) of INPUT, which is a guess: the right place for a table boundary is where the symbol distribution changes. Token decisions and the rep-distance state are fixed before the emit, so a block's encoded size depends only on its own tokens - which makes the partition a shortest path. Prefix histograms of the emitted symbols at every candidate boundary (a 64 KiB grid plus the fixed layout's own cuts, spans capped at 512 KiB) price any block exactly from two snapshots, a shortest path picks the partition, and each boundary is then moved within +/-32 KiB on a 4 KiB grid by coordinate descent over its two adjacent blocks' exact costs, twice. The cost model counts what `encode_token_block` writes and nothing else - the table description at the member's `algorithm_version` (so RAR 7's 80 distance slots are priced as 80), the leading filter records the first block carries (their symbol 256 folded into the main histogram BEFORE the code lengths are built, their raw payload counted by writing it rather than by a second copy of the field widths), and the block framing - and `statistical_cost_matches_actual_emission` pins it to the emitter over both distance tables and three filter sets. The fixed layout is PRICED by the same model rather than encoded, so only the winner is ever emitted; it is kept as the fallback and a release-mode guard re-emits it if the emitted length ever exceeded the fixed price, so the output can never grow. The prefix snapshots (a 4 KiB grid over 4 MiB is ~1,000 of ~3.5 KB) live in `EncoderScratch` and `LiveSpanEncoder` for the reason the match index does. `ENTROPY_BLOCK_MIN_TOKENS` stays on `entropy_block_token_ranges`, which cuts by input bytes and cannot know what a table costs, and is deliberately NOT a constraint on the search, which is measured rather than assumed: imposing it cost -0.27% instead of -0.76% on the mixed corpus at 32 MiB and -0.58% instead of -1.34% at 128 KiB, and the repeated-payload corpus - the case the floor was added for - came out 919 bytes SMALLER without it. Refused by name rather than silently dropped: a percent without the feature flag or the flag without a percent (`validate_recovery_request`), a RAR 1.5 or 2.0 target (those want the old-style `PROTECT_HEAD` block), a header-encrypted archive (the record would be written in the clear and `newsub_recovery_data` declines an encrypted one), and a VOLUME set (`rar` writes one record per volume over that volume's own bytes; `validate_volume_writer_inputs` refuses, because the volume writers share the single-archive validators and would otherwise pass and write nothing). The percentage rule is `plan_inline_recovery`'s, floored, so one `recovery_record_pct` means the same on both generations; `rar 7.23` rounds instead, measured on a 391-sector archive at 4/8/12/19/39/78/117/195 against this rule's 3/7/11/19/39/78/117/195. Ten tests, and the one that matters is `rar4_recovery_record_we_wrote_is_repaired_by_winrar` in `tests/winrar_recovery.rs`: RARLab's own `rar` finds the record, names the damaged sector from our tags and rebuilds the file byte-exact. **NOT synced**: hand-made here, for the reason the two rows above give - vendor/ is ahead of the upstream rars fork on many files and `sync-from-fork.sh` would rsync `--delete` an older engine over them. | `src/recovery/rar3.rs`, `src/rar15_40.rs`, `src/rar15_40/write.rs`, `src/lib.rs`, `tests/integration/winrar_recovery.rs` |

## Deep gate before a release (decoder changes especially)

The `--lib` gate above and the fuzzers use small inputs, so they are blind to
size-dependent decode bugs: back-references reaching past the streaming window
(>64 MiB), solid cross-member history, and volume-split members only appear in
large real archives. The fork carries a real-`rar` round-trip rig for exactly
these axes at `crates/rars/tests/real_archive_diff.rs`. It is NOT vendored (a
`tests/*.rs` file) and needs a local `rar` 7.x, so run it in the fork checkout
before cutting a release or dropping the external `unrar` fallback:

```sh
cargo test -p rars --test real_archive_diff -- --ignored --nocapture
```

It builds ~76 MiB archives across RAR5/RAR7 dictionary sizes (128 MiB..1 GiB),
solid multi-file sets, and multivolume splits, and asserts rars decodes each
byte-for-byte. This is what would have caught the 64 MiB streaming-window cap.

The whole export ships in the public repo (`vendor` is in
`packaging/PUBLIC_MANIFEST`; `/vendor/` is leak-scan-exempt as third-party
source), which satisfies build-from-source.
